title: Stage 9, Lesson 5: Managing consumer debt - car loans, credit cards, cash loans
subtitle: Not every debt deserves to be paid off at the same speed
openingQuestion: You hold two debts: a credit card at 35% a year with 20 million outstanding, and a mortgage at 9% a year with 2 billion outstanding. With 20 million spare, which should you pay down first?
openingOptions: The mortgage, because the balance is far larger
The credit card, because 35% a year dwarfs 9%
Split it evenly, 10 million each, to be fair
Neither - put the whole 20 million into investments instead
explanation: The rule for optimal repayment: clear the HIGHEST interest rate first (the avalanche method), whatever the absolute balances are. Vietnamese credit card rates usually run 20-40% a year - far above almost any safe investment - so paying down a card is nearly always the highest-returning "investment" available for spare cash.

diagram.label: List every debt with its interest rate
Sort by interest rate, highest first
Pay the minimum on all, put the surplus on the highest rate
Repeat until the high-rate debt is gone

realWorldExample.description: Vietnamese credit card rates, where the balance is not cleared within the interest-free window (usually 45-55 days), typically run 20-40% a year - far above savings rates or most investment returns, which makes carrying a card balance one of the most expensive financial decisions available.

quiz.question: Why does clearing a credit card balance within the interest-free window matter so much more than with other kinds of borrowing?
options: Because credit card interest is charged daily on the balance outstanding
Because no interest applies inside the window, and it is very high outside it
Because paying on time makes the bank raise the card limit
Because the annual fee is waived if you pay in full each month
quiz.explanation: What makes credit cards distinct is the very high rate (20-40% a year) that applies as soon as the interest-free window closes on an unpaid balance - which is why carrying a card balance is usually far more expensive than a secured loan such as a mortgage or a car loan.

quiz.question: How do the "avalanche" method (highest rate first) and the "snowball" method (smallest balance first) differ, and when is snowball worth choosing even though it costs more interest mathematically?
options: The two methods produce exactly the same outcome
Snowball optimises interest while avalanche optimises psychology
Snowball optimises psychology; avalanche optimises interest
Avalanche can only be used with fewer than three debts
quiz.explanation: Avalanche is mathematically optimal (it saves the most interest), but snowball has a psychological advantage: clearing one small debt gives a visible win that helps some people stay with the overall plan - at the cost of slightly more interest in theory.

quiz.question: You have 20 million spare, a credit card balance at 30% a year, and the option of a savings account at 6% a year. Which is better arithmetically?
options: Save it: keeping cash on hand in case of an emergency
Split it: 10 million on the debt and 10 million into savings
Save it: because deposit interest is exempt from personal income tax
Pay down the card: avoid 6 million of interest rather than earn 1.2
quiz.explanation: Avoiding a certain cost of 30% a year beats earning 6% a year by a wide margin. The only real consideration is keeping something back for the emergency fund - not the rate comparison.

quiz.question: Why can a 0% instalment plan still be expensive?
options: Because it usually carries a conversion fee charged on the full value
Because the instalment price is always set higher than the outright cash price
Because the 0% rate only applies for the first three months
Because you have to open another credit card to be approved
quiz.explanation: The only reliable check is to reduce it to a total: add up every instalment plus every fee, then compare against the price for paying outright.

quiz.question: How does taking cash from a credit card differ from paying for goods with it?
options: The same rate applies, but the interest-free period is cut in half
Interest runs from the day of withdrawal with no interest-free period, plus a withdrawal fee
There is no difference, since both sit inside the same credit limit
It carries a lower rate, because handing over cash is a simpler form of disbursement
quiz.explanation: The interest-free window only applies to purchases. Cash taken from a card is charged interest from day one plus a withdrawal fee of a few per cent - making it one of the most expensive sources of money an individual can reach.

keyTakeaways: Clear the highest-rate debt first (avalanche), whatever the absolute balances are
Vietnamese credit card rates (20-40% a year) are far above most other borrowing - clear the balance inside the interest-free window
The snowball method (smallest balance first) has a psychological edge and suits people who need the momentum

practicePrompt.question: You have three debts: a credit card of 20 million at 30% a year, a consumer loan of 50 million at 15% a year, and a car loan of 100 million at 9% a year. With another 10 million to put towards debt, which should it go to (avalanche method)?
options: The car loan (100 million) first, because it carries the largest absolute balance of the three
The highest interest rate first, which is the credit card at 30% a year
Split the 10 million across all three in proportion to their balances, to be fair between the loans
The consumer loan (50 million), because it sits in the middle of the three balances
practicePrompt.explanation: Pay the highest interest rate first, whatever the absolute balance is. Vietnamese credit card rates (20-40% a year) are far above most other borrowing - so clear the balance inside the interest-free window.

application.title: Rank your debts by their real rate
application.message: List everything you are repaying and write the real rate beside it - a 0% instalment through a card still carries a conversion fee, and a consumer loan quoted monthly has to be multiplied up. Sort the list downwards, then put every spare dong on the top line and the minimum on the rest.
application.secondary: If the list is so long you cannot start, clear the smallest one first for momentum. Discipline you can sustain is worth more than a few percentage points computed exactly.

sections.text: Not every debt deserves the same priority - knowing which one to clear first can save you a great deal of interest.
The avalanche rule: highest interest rate first

The avalanche rule clears the highest rate first, whatever the absolute balances are. The snowball method (smallest balance first) costs more interest mathematically, but carries a psychological advantage that helps keep the repayment going.

sections.title: Why clearing high-rate debt is the best "investment" available
sections.equation: Benefit of paying down = Amount repaid × That debt's interest rate

variables.name: The rate you are being charged
variables.description: Every dong repaid is a dong no longer charged at that rate - a certain benefit, with no risk attached.

example.title: A direct comparison
example.calculation: 10 million against a card at 30% a year vs 10 million into savings at 5% a year
example.result: 3 million of interest saved a year vs 500 thousand earned a year
example.explanation: Paying the card down returns six times as much, and it is certain and risk-free. This is why there is almost no reason to hold spare cash while carrying a credit card balance.

left.label: Avalanche - highest rate first
left.text: Sort the debts by interest rate, highest first, and put every spare dong on the top one while paying the minimum on the rest. Mathematically this saves the most interest.

right.label: Snowball - smallest balance first
right.text: Put the money on the smallest balance to clear it quickly and get a sense of completion. It costs more interest, but it keeps many people going to the end.

items: 0% instalments: the rate is zero, but there is usually a conversion fee charged on the full value. Reduce it to a total and compare against buying outright.
Cash from a credit card: a fee applies immediately and interest runs from the day of withdrawal, with none of the interest-free window a purchase gets.
Paying only the minimum for a long time: the minimum usually covers the interest and a very small slice of principal, so the balance barely moves while the interest keeps running.

sections.label: The order to work in with several debts
sections.text: One: list every debt with its balance, rate and minimum payment. Two: make sure every minimum is paid on time so nothing slips into a worse debt group. Three: put all the remaining money on a single debt - the highest rate. Four: when that one is cleared, move the whole freed-up amount to the next one rather than raising your spending.

lines: Clearing a credit card on time is nearly always the highest-returning "investment" available for spare cash.
There is no safe investment paying 20-40% a year to compare it against.

summary.keyIdea: Clear the highest-rate debt first (avalanche), whatever the absolute balances are
